solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: My family home collects different food to barbecue here? (3,2,5)

indicators.note: to collect is to gather in, so OURS takes the other letters inside it
FOOD TO made different is FOOD TO in another order

blocks.note: the home of my family is ours, as in 'come round to ours'
FOOD TO rearranged, placed inside OU…RS

annotation.surface: Someone boasts that their family's house takes in all sorts of food, ideal for a barbecue.
annotation.walkthrough: OURS as a home is the hard step. The 'to' looks like a link into the definition but belongs to the anagram fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: barbecues are cooked outside, so the place for one is in the open air.

entries.clue: My bad theatre job, enormous curtains (4)

indicators.note: curtains hang either side of a stage, so OS frames OP

blocks.note: OS = outsize, the clothing size
an op, an operation, is the job done in an operating theatre

annotation.surface: A critic sighs over a dreadful stage production with vast curtains.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive attached to 'bad theatre job', but 'My bad' is the slang apology, and the theatre is a hospital's.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are interjections for owning up to a small slip; 'my bad' is the newer American slang.

entries.clue: Worked beside well (4)

blocks.note: to = against, next to, as in 'cheek to cheek'
OK = well, fine

annotation.surface: Someone laboured next to a well.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Worked' mean laboured; the sense wanted is succeeded.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of taking effect: a graft or an injection that took did its job.

entries.clue: Silly exploit with plant that flavours water (7-5)

definitions.note: 'Silly' here is the noun, a silly person, matching the noun FEATHERBRAIN

blocks.note: an exploit is a feat
a herb is a plant used for flavouring
water falling from the sky

annotation.surface: A daft stunt involving a herb used to flavour drinking water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'plant that flavours water' reads as one phrase about herbal infusions, but the water is a separate piece, from the sky.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Silly' used as a noun, as in 'you silly', names a scatterbrained person.

entries.clue: Broadcasting / very happily? (2,3)

blocks.note: the studio phrase for a programme going out live
cut down from the idiom 'walking on …' for being overjoyed

annotation.walkthrough: The second sense lops 'walking' off the idiom, which is why it carries a question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: A studio sign lights up when transmitting; and someone walking on air is elated.

entries.clue: Fish / a curious topping for ginger nut? (3,6)

definitions.text: a curious topping for ginger nut?

blocks.note: a pink-red Mediterranean food fish

blocks.clueFragment: a curious topping for ginger nut?
blocks.note: ginger = red hair, nut = head, and the curious topping is the short-front, long-back haircut

annotation.surface: Someone wonders what odd sprinkle to put on a ginger nut biscuit.
annotation.walkthrough: A ginger nut is a British ginger biscuit, but here ginger is hair colour and the nut is the head. A mullet is the short-at-the-front, long-at-the-back haircut.
annotation.definitionFit: The fish is named for its colour; the hairstyle reading is a cryptic second sense on a redhead.

entries.clue: Hot green dresses are imitations (4)

definitions.note: 'imitations' is plural; ECHO is its singular

indicators.note: to dress something is to clothe it, so ECO wraps round H

blocks.note: eco- = environmentally friendly, green
H = hot, as on a tap

annotation.surface: Fashionable green frocks turn out to be copies.
annotation.walkthrough: 'dresses' looks like a noun in a fashion story but is the verb. The definition is plural where the answer is singular, a loose fit.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a repeated sound or style copies its original.

entries.clue: Result of a little home cooking? (7,3)

definitions.text: Result of a little home cooking?

blocks.note: the surface reads a small amount of home cooking; the setter means a small house
what the cooking produces is a baked dish named after that small house

annotation.surface: A simple dish made in the kitchen at home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Little home' is to be read as a cottage, not as a modest amount of home cooking. Cottage pie is minced beef topped with mashed potato.
annotation.definitionFit: The dish takes its name from the humble rural dwelling, so it is literally what cooking a small home yields.

entries.clue: Confining serpent’s victim to pit below not awfully fair (2,3,5)

indicators.note: to confine is to shut in, so HELL shuts EVE inside it
in a down clue, HELL sits below the rearranged NOT
NOT done awfully is NOT done badly, out of order

blocks.note: NOT rearranged
the pit = hell
the serpent tempted her in Eden

annotation.surface: An image of a snake's prey being thrown into a pit, which is hardly fair.
annotation.walkthrough: The serpent is the one in Genesis. 'Pit below not' works only in a down entry, where the pit hangs under the rearranged NOT.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from carpentry, where a level surface is true, meaning honest and above board.

entries.clue: Promotional material mentioned genuine East End butcher’s? (10)

indicators.note: to mention is to say, so the words are spoken, not spelt
London's East End is Cockney country, and this is the Cockney pronunciation

blocks.note: proper = genuine, said the Cockney way
a butcher's is a look (rhyming slang: butcher's hook), and so is a gander

annotation.surface: An advert boasting of a genuine East London butcher's shop.
annotation.walkthrough: Butcher's is Cockney rhyming slang: butcher's hook = look, and a gander is also a look. A 'proper gander' in an East End accent drops the final Rs.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though propaganda carries the sense of biased or misleading promotion.

entries.clue: A little bird doing no good (2,2)

blocks.note: read as two words: A plus a small garden bird
the idiom for someone up to mischief again

annotation.surface: A small bird up to mischief.
annotation.walkthrough: The first sense only works split as A + TIT; the enumeration (2,2) hides that.
annotation.definitionFit: The first is literal, the bird being a tit; the second is the idiom 'at it again', said of misbehaviour.

entries.clue: Station café’s offering things to give ox (7,5)

blocks.note: cha (char) is British slang for tea
draw a circle and you get the letter O; draw a diagonal x-shape and you get X

annotation.surface: A station café serving something meant to feed an ox.
annotation.walkthrough: 'ox' is not the animal but two letters, O and X, each made by a shape. Charing Cross is a London railway station.
annotation.definitionFit: A proper name: one of London's mainline railway termini.

entries.clue: Love, difficult at a distance, gets in the way (12)

indicators.note: to get in is to enter, so the three pieces enter THE

blocks.note: the word itself, split round the other pieces
love = O, a zero score in tennis
a rough time is a difficult one
far = at a distance

annotation.surface: Someone complains that a long-distance love affair just gets in the way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'gets in the way' reads as one idiom, but it splits into the container instruction, a piece of wordplay, and the one-word definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym: a thoroughfare is a public road, a way through.

entries.clue: Spring routine restricted by extremely elaborate footwear (10)

indicators.note: to be restricted is to be hemmed in, so SPA DRILL sits inside
the extremes of 'elaborate' are its first and last letters

blocks.note: the outer letters of ElaboratE
a spa is a mineral spring
a drill is a set routine

annotation.surface: A spring exercise routine is constrained by some very fancy shoes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spring' suggests the season or a leap; here it is a place with a mineral spring.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the espadrille is a canvas shoe with a rope sole.

entries.clue: Children had remained with English housekeeper (10)

blocks.note: ch. = children, as in dictionary abbreviations
had a meal = ate
past participle of lie, to remain lying
E = English

annotation.surface: The children had stayed behind with an English housekeeper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'had remained' reads as one verb phrase but is two past forms: had a meal, and stayed lying.
annotation.definitionFit: The mistress of a large house, who traditionally carried its keys on a chain at her waist.

entries.clue: Charlie’s excitedly welcoming Penny round (9)

indicators.note: letters that are excited are stirred up, out of order
to welcome is to take in, so the rearranged letters take P inside

blocks.note: CHARLIES rearranged, split round P
p = penny

annotation.surface: Charlie greets Penny enthusiastically as she comes round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'round' at the end looks like part of Penny's visit, but it is the definition, an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym: ball-shaped is round in three dimensions.

entries.clue: Covering between 100 and 1000 substantial cycles (9)

indicators.note: the cycled word sits between C and M
a cycle goes round, so FILLING's end comes round to the front

blocks.note: C = 100 in Roman numerals
FILLING (substantial, of a meal) cycled
M = 1000 in Roman numerals

annotation.surface: Some covering measures between a hundred and a thousand big turns.
annotation.walkthrough: 'cycles' looks like a noun counting revolutions, but it is the instruction to rotate the word. Clingfilm is the British name for plastic food wrap.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the stretchy plastic wrap is a covering for food.

entries.clue: Member of party departing the Tabard Inn, where everybody’s drunk (5)

definitions.text: Member of party departing the Tabard Inn

indicators.note: something drunk is taken in, so the words have swallowed the answer

blocks.note: wheRE EVErybody's

annotation.surface: A pilgrim leaves a pub where everyone is drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales the pilgrims set off from the Tabard Inn in Southwark. 'drunk' reads as tipsy but means swallowed.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary allusion: one of Chaucer's pilgrims tells the Reeve's Tale.

entries.clue: Noisily change focal point of service (5)

indicators.note: something done noisily is heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: alter = change

annotation.surface: A loud reorganisation of the heart of a church service.
annotation.walkthrough: 'service' could be at a restaurant or in tennis; it is a church service.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the communion table is where worship is centred.

entries.clue: Metrically, one’s very rigorous (9)

blocks.note: the metric system counts in tens
one has = I have, contracted

annotation.surface: In verse, someone declares themselves a strict stickler.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Metrically' suggests poetry metre; it means by the metric system. The 's of 'one's' is 'has', not a possessive.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym, as in an intensive course: concentrated and demanding.

entries.clue: Buffet cars inter alia currently serving rich gravy (7,5)

definitions.text: Buffet cars inter alia currently serving

blocks.note: rolling = very rich, as in rolling in it
the meat juices gravy is made from

annotation.surface: The dining car on a train is now dishing up thick gravy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Buffet cars' set a catering scene, but they are railway carriages, and 'currently serving' means in use on the line.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a railway's vehicles in service include its buffet cars.

entries.clue: Chap out on roof newly illuminated from the ground? (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, reading from the ground up turns the word over

blocks.note: lit again

annotation.surface: A man on the roof is lit up by floodlights from below.
annotation.walkthrough: 'from the ground' belongs to the lighting in the surface but tells you to read upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the tradesman who lays roof tiles works up there.

entries.clue: Step out of a prison (4)

indicators.note: 'out of' means leaving something behind: the step goes out of its A

blocks.note: a stair is a step
the letter taken out

annotation.surface: An instruction to walk out of a jail.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Step out' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'out of' is the deletion.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang for jail, as in 'doing time in stir'.

entries.clue: Group One beginning to have change of heart (4)

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, and here those middle letters change places

blocks.note: a tiro (tyro) is a beginner

annotation.surface: A band's first member is starting to have second thoughts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Group One' looks like a label, but 'One beginning' is a beginner, whose middle two letters swap.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: three players or singers form a small group.

entries.clue: Current stable employee covers bet (4)

indicators.note: to cover something is to go over and around it, so LAD sits either side of I

blocks.note: a stable lad looks after racehorses
I = electric current, in physics

annotation.surface: A racing stable hand places a wager at today's odds.
annotation.walkthrough: The racing picture makes 'bet' a noun; it is the past tense, as in laid a bet.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym in betting language: to lay money is to stake it.

entries.clue: Queen Elizabeth Gates perhaps showing this sticker? (10)

blocks.note: Bill Gates, founder of Microsoft
Gates is written after the Queen, and post = after
Elizabeth Regina

annotation.surface: Some royal gates bearing a notice.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads its own word order: Gates is placed after the Queen, and that relation spells the answer. Queen Elizabeth Gate is also a real gate in Hyde Park, London.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal reading: someone who sticks up posters is a sticker.

entries.clue: Love interest of old city MD? (4)

blocks.note: a former partner
EC is the postcode of the City of London

annotation.surface: A romance in an old city with a doctor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'old city' pulls toward Exeter or Ur, but 'of old' goes with the love interest. MD is managing director, not a doctor.
annotation.definitionFit: A managing director is a senior executive; the answer is the short form.

entries.clue: Play I promise a short run in? (10)

definitions.text: Play I promise a short run in?

indicators.note: letters at play move about, so I PROMISE is rearranged
A and R go in the rearranged letters

blocks.note: I PROMISE rearranged, split round AR
the letter itself
R = run, in cricket scoring

annotation.surface: A theatre producer assures us the show will have only a brief run.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also something a theatrical producer might say about a new show.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is a producer's line about staging a show for a limited season.
